title: Associations Between Male Partner Participation, Women’s Autonomy, and Postpartum Care Seeking Among First Time Mothers, 15-24 Years, in Kinshasa, DRC: A Cross-Sectional Analysis
content: The Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) has both a high maternal and neonatal mortality rate and only a third of mothers and newborns have a postpartum care visit. Increasing male participation and enhancing women’s autonomy are programmatic strategies to increase maternal healthcare utilization but the applicability among first-time mothers (FTMs) in Kinshasa, DRC is unknown. We conducted a secondary analysis using cross-sectional survey data from a maternal and child health project among FTMs and their male partners in Kinshasa, DRC. The sample consisted of 1,750 FTMs 15-24 years. The outcome variables were: (1) a postpartum care visit within six weeks of facility discharge for the mother, (2) a postnatal care visit within six weeks of facility discharge for the neonate, and (3) either a postnatal or postpartum care visit within six weeks of facility discharge. Two logistic multivariate regression models were run for each outcome. The first model included all explanatory and demographic variables, and the second model added two interaction terms to test for mediation by in-union status and age. The male participation in maternal care index was negatively associated with all outcomes and the male participation in childcare index was positively associated with all outcomes. In-union status mediated the relationship between the male involvement indexes and postpartum care for the mother but not for postnatal care for the newborn. Our findings show that the type of male participation may be meaningful for increasing postpartum and postnatal care-seeking and male partner participation initiatives need to be contextualized to prevent adverse outcomes.
